name: Ampliatus
title: Paul's beloved in the Lord
summary: Ampliatus was a believer in Rome whom Paul greeted by name in the letter to the Romans. With the warm designation 'my beloved in the Lord', Paul expressed a close personal and spiritual bond with Ampliatus, suggesting that the two knew each other beforehand – perhaps from another city in the Roman Empire, since Paul had not yet visited Rome when the letter was written. The name Ampliatus occurred very frequently among slaves and freedmen in the imperial households, which may offer a clue about his social background. In the Domitilla catacombs in Rome, a richly decorated burial chamber from the end of the first century bearing this name has been found, a discovery that has fascinated scholars, even though a definite connection to the biblical Ampliatus cannot be proven. Ampliatus' presence in Paul's list of greetings testifies to the diverse composition of the early church, where social divisions were overcome in fellowship with Christ.
roles: Paul's personal friend and fellow believer

keyEvents.title: Greeting from Paul
keyEvents.description: Paul mentions Ampliatus by name in his letter to the Romans, calling him 'my beloved in the Lord'. The personal phrasing stands out in the greeting list and testifies to a deep, mutual relationship—likely established before Paul wrote to the church in Rome. The greeting places Ampliatus within a community marked by love and mutual care across geographical and social boundaries.

versions.title: Beloved brother in the Lord
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'servant' is not directly confirmed in the Bible for Ampliatus. Although the name was common among slaves and freedmen, the text does not explicitly state that he was a servant. 'Christian in Rome' would be a more precise role. 'Disciple' is acceptable as a general term but could be replaced with something more specific such as 'member of the church in Rome'.; [minor] The title 'Beloved brother in the Lord' is good, but the Greek text uses the expression 'my beloved in the Lord' (τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ). The term 'brother' is not explicitly mentioned in the verse, although it is implied in a Christian context. 'Paul's beloved in the Lord' may be more faithful to the text.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are interesting historical, archaeological, and linguistic details that should be covered – for example, about the name Ampliatus in Roman catacombs, the origin of the name among slaves/freedmen, and the possible connection to the Catacomb of Domitilla.

footnotes.text: The name Ampliatus (Latin: Ampliatus, meaning 'expanded' or 'great') was very common among slaves and freedmen in the Roman Empire. It appears frequently in inscriptions from imperial households, leading to speculation that he may have belonged to Caesar's household (cf. Phil 4:22).

In the Domitilla catacombs in Rome, there is a burial chamber from the end of the 1st century with the name 'AMPLIATUS' written in an unusually decorated style suggesting high status. Some scholars have proposed a connection to the Ampliatus mentioned in Romans, although this cannot be confirmed with certainty.

When Paul calls Ampliatus 'my beloved in the Lord' (Greek: τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ) using the personal pronoun 'my', it suggests a personal acquaintance rather than just a general Christian greeting. This is remarkable since Paul himself had not visited Rome when he wrote the letter, indicating that they knew each other from another place.

According to Eastern church tradition, Ampliatus is regarded as one of the seventy disciples and is said to have become bishop in Odyssos (today's Varna in Bulgaria). This tradition cannot be historically verified, but it shows that early Christians attributed a more important role to him than what appears from Romans alone.

Romans chapter 16 contains an unusually long list of personal greetings – about 26 people are mentioned by name. This provides unique insight into the diverse network of Christians in early Rome, where people from various social classes – slaves, freedmen, and free citizens – formed one community in faith.
